messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Kwame is a 45-year-old African American man who has spent most of his adult life doing agricultural work, moving through long days of irrigation lines, machinery noise, and the exposed distances of open fields. When he speaks about why he has come for help now, he does not begin with the present. He goes back to a house from his childhood, to nights when he would hear his mother and the man who lived with them fighting behind a closed door. The worst memory is one he returns to unwillingly but in sharp fragments: his mother being thrown against the kitchen wall, a chair scraping hard across the floor, the sound of her crying out, and himself standing nearby, frozen and useless. He remembers the yellow kitchen light, the tightness in his chest, and the certainty that something terrible was happening while he did nothing that mattered. What remains most unbearable for him is not only what he saw, but the conviction he carries that he failed her. He says, in different ways, that he should have done more, should have stepped in, should have stopped it somehow, even though he was only a child.

In the years afterward, Kwame did not speak much about those nights. He tried to force the memories away whenever they came up, pushing his mind toward work, chores, anything else. If an image broke through anyway, he would clamp down harder, telling himself not to think about it. But the effort never gave him peace. He found himself turning over the same thoughts for hours, especially at night, imagining ways he might have gotten even with the man who hurt his mother. Even now, decades later, his mind can get pulled into those revenge fantasies with a grim, repetitive logic, as if he is still trying to settle something unfinished. He does not describe these thoughts with satisfaction. They leave him tense and bitter, and afterward he feels even further from the person he believes he used to be.

Kwame says he was once a happy person, or at least he remembers there being an easier version of himself. Now he experiences himself as permanently miserable, a man who has lost something central and cannot get it back. He has also come to believe that faith itself has gone out of his life. He does not mean only religious faith, though that too has dimmed. More broadly, he no longer trusts people, life, or reassurances of any kind. If someone tells him he is safe, he feels almost irritated by the statement, because inside it does not register as real. He is certain that safety can disappear too quickly to be believed in.

That sense is with him every day in the fields. Agricultural work often requires men to move in and out of trucks, storage sheds, and irrigation areas together, and Kwame has developed a firm rule for himself: he tries never to be alone with another person. He does not announce this rule, but he organizes himself around it. If a coworker asks him to check equipment in a barn or walk a fence line without others nearby, he finds a reason to delay, brings someone else along, or avoids the task if he can. In his own mind this is simply prudent. Being alone with one other person feels exposed, unpredictable, too much like being trapped close to someone whose intentions he cannot fully know. This has made him seem distant and difficult at work. Supervisors have noticed that he hesitates with certain assignments, and coworkers sometimes read his behavior as unfriendly. At home, his partner has also felt the strain. Kwame keeps watch rather than relaxing, especially after dark, scanning sounds outside the house, checking locks again, staying alert deep into the night. Nighttime feels distinctly less safe to him than daytime; darkness sharpens his expectation that something could happen without warning.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become harder to contain. His partner had told him that he never seems at ease, that even in ordinary evenings he looks like a man waiting for danger. Kwame recognized the truth of that. He is tired of living on guard and tired of being pulled into old scenes he tries so hard not to think about. What finally brought him in was not a single crisis but the accumulating weight of misery, distrust, and guilt. He is afraid that this is simply who he is now: a man who cannot feel safe, cannot trust anyone’s reassurance, and cannot forgive himself for freezing when his mother needed him. At the same time, he is hoping, cautiously, that talking about it might loosen the grip of those nights enough for him to stop living as if they are still happening.
